name: Breathing Difficulty
source_guidance: Adapted from NHS 111 guidance on shortness of breath and anaphylaxis, and WHO guidance on acute respiratory illness and tuberculosis screening.

questions.text: Is the person struggling to breathe, or unable to say more than a few words at a time?
Are the lips, tongue, or face blue or grey, or is the person confused or very drowsy?
Did the breathing problem start suddenly with swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or after a sting, food, or medicine?
Is there chest pain together with the breathing difficulty?
Is the person short of breath while resting, or is their usual inhaler not helping?
Is there a fever with cough and fast breathing?
Has a cough lasted more than two weeks, or is there night sweats or weight loss?

emergency: Call 112 now, or get to the nearest hospital emergency department immediately.
Help the person sit upright, leaning slightly forward. Loosen tight clothing.
If they have an adrenaline auto-injector for allergy, use it now.
If they have a reliever inhaler, they can use it while waiting.
Do not drive yourself. Ask someone to take you, or wait for the ambulance.
urgent: Go to a hospital or clinic today and be seen within the next few hours.
Use the reliever inhaler as prescribed while travelling.
Call 112 if lips turn blue or grey or the person cannot speak in full sentences.
routine: Book a clinic appointment within the next few days and ask for a tuberculosis (TB) test.
Cover the mouth when coughing and keep the room well aired.
Call back at once if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.
self_care: The answers point to a mild breathing complaint, such as a common cold.
Rest, drink plenty of fluids, and keep the room well aired.
Paracetamol can be taken as directed on the pack for fever or aches.
Call back at once if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.
